hook.line: The year French mathematician Édouard Lucas published this game — a “mathematician’s game” you play with just paper and pencil.
hook.say: A history that starts in the margin of a notebook!

p: In 1889 Lucas introduced it as “La Pipopipette”, said to have been played by students of the École Polytechnique in Paris.
In the 20th century the mathematician Elwyn Berlekamp wrote a whole book on how to win it.

tl: Strategy analysed in the classic “Winning Ways”
Berlekamp publishes “The Dots and Boxes Game”
The 4×5 board is analysed by computer

ch.t: Draw the fourth side, claim the box
ch.say: Close a box and you draw again!
ch.cap: Draw one line at a time; completing the fourth side wins the box
p: Players take turns joining two dots; whoever draws a box’s fourth side claims it.
Claiming a box earns another move — so when to hand over a “chain” decides the game.

cards: Variants on triangular or hexagonal dot grids

ch.say: Even a small board has lots of lines!
stats: Lines that can be drawn on it
cards: French mathematician also known for Fibonacci-number research and the Tower of Hanoi
A giant of combinatorial game theory who systematised how to win this game

ch.say: Tap a card to flip it!
cards: The parity of long chains often decides who is ahead
Ever give boxes away on purpose?
Yes — handing over two boxes to win a big chain later is a classic trick

ch.say: Which way will you pass the chain?
p: Between the dots lies a mathematician’s wisdom.
